'''Victor Malka''' (born 1960 in [[Casablanca|Casablanca, Morocco]]) is a French plasma [[physicist]] and a pioneer in [[Laser Plasma Acceleration|laser plasma acceleration]]. In 2004, Malka demonstrated that high energy monoenergetic [[electron beams]] could be generated using the technique of [[laser wakefield acceleration]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Faure|first1=J.|last2=Glinec|first2=Y.|last3=Pukhov|first3=A.|last4=Kiselev|first4=S.|last5=Gordienko|first5=S.|last6=Lefebvre|first6=E.|last7=Rousseau|first7=J.-P.|last8=Burgy|first8=F.|last9=Malka|first9=V.|s2cid=4363528|date=2004|title=A laser–plasma accelerator producing monoenergetic electron beams|url=http://www.nature.com/articles/nature02963|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=431|issue=7008|pages=541–544|doi=10.1038/nature02963|pmid=15457253|bibcode=2004Natur.431..541F|issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and subsequently used them to develop compact [[X-ray]] and [[Gamma Radiation|gamma radiation]] sources with applications in [[medicine]], security technology and [[phase-contrast imaging]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Malka|first1=Victor|last2=Faure|first2=Jérôme|last3=Gauduel|first3=Yann A.|last4=Lefebvre|first4=Erik|last5=Rousse|first5=Antoine|last6=Phuoc|first6=Kim Ta|date=2008|title=Principles and applications of compact laser–plasma accelerators|journal=Nature Physics|volume=4|issue=6|pages=447–453|doi=10.1038/nphys966|bibcode=2008NatPh...4..447M|issn=1745-2473}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ta Phuoc|first1=K.|last2=Corde|first2=S.|last3=Thaury|first3=C.|last4=Malka|first4=V.|last5=Tafzi|first5=A.|last6=Goddet|first6=J. == Early life and career ==
{{unsourced BLP section|date=June 2020}}
Malka came from a Jewish family in [[Morocco]] and came to [[France]] at the age of six, where he grew up in [[Marseille]] and in the Parisian suburbs. He studied at the Ecole nationale supérieure de chimie in Rennes and received his doctorate at the [[École Polytechnique]] with a dissertation in atomic and [[Plasma (physics)|plasma physics]]. From 1990, he then worked at the École Polytechnique for the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (CNRS), and from 2004 as Research Director of the Laboratory for Applied Optics (LOA). From 2003 to 2015, he was a professor at the École Polytechnique. He has been a professor at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] since 2015.
